title: Saul, David and Solomon
bigQuestion: What do the books of Samuel and Kings say a good king should be, and what happens when kings fall short?

story.title: A Harp for a Troubled King
story.kicker: A shepherd boy walks into a palace with a harp, and the king cannot stop listening.
paragraphs: The king sat in his chair and stared at the wall. His name was Saul. He was the first king Israel ever had. He was tall and strong, but lately his mind was dark and heavy. His servants whispered. "Music might help," one said. "There is a boy in Bethlehem who plays the harp."

The boy's name was David. He was the youngest of eight brothers. He spent his days on the hills with his father's sheep. He knew how to sling a stone at a wolf. He also knew how to play a harp until the sheep lay down calm. Now a messenger stood at his door. "The king wants you," he said.

David walked into the palace with the harp on his back. He did not look at the gold or the guards. He sat down near the king and began to play. The notes were soft and slow. The king's shoulders dropped. He closed his eyes. For the first time in days, he could breathe.

The book of Samuel says Saul loved David and made him his armor-bearer. It also says that whenever the dark mood came back, David played, and the king felt better. Neither of them knew what the story would say next. One day the boy with the harp would wear the crown himself.

Jewish tradition still connects David with music. Many of the Psalms carry his name at the top. Some are sung in synagogues in Chicago every week. A song that once calmed one troubled king is still being sung.
story.think: Why do you think the story introduces David with a harp before it shows him with a sword?

lessons.title: The People Want a King
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Samuel says the people asked for a king, and Samuel warned them what a king would cost.
reading: For a long time, the book of Judges says, Israel had no king. Leaders called judges stepped up when trouble came. Then they went home. The last of these leaders was *Samuel*. He was a prophet and a judge. When Samuel grew old, the leaders of the people came to him with a request.

"Give us a king," they said, "like all the other nations." The book of *1 Samuel*, chapter 8, tells this scene. Samuel did not like the idea. The text says he prayed, and God told him to listen to the people but to warn them first.

Samuel gave a warning. A king would take their sons for his army. He would take their daughters as cooks and bakers. He would take the best of their fields and flocks. The people still said yes. Jewish tradition reads this as a story about what people give up when they want to be like everyone else.

words.d: a prophet and the last judge of Israel; he chose the first two kings
a book of the Nevi'im that tells how Israel got its first kings
a ruler who leads a whole people and passes the crown to a child

look.title: Samuel's Warning
look.text: Samuel tells the people what a king will do. He will take your sons to drive his chariots and run before him. He will take your daughters to make perfume and bake bread. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards. And one day you will cry out because of the king you chose.
look.cite: 1 Samuel 8:11-18, Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What is the biggest cost Samuel says a king will bring? Why do you think the people said yes anyway?

check.q: Who was the last judge of Israel before there was a king?
check.why: The book of 1 Samuel says Samuel was a prophet and the last judge. He chose the first kings.

check.q: Why did the people say they wanted a king?
choices: To be like all the other nations
check.why: In 1 Samuel 8 the people say, "like all the other nations." That is the reason the text gives.

check.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take their sons, daughters, fields and flocks
check.why: Samuel's warning lists what a king would take. The people still chose a king.

lessons.title: Saul, the Tall, Shy King
lessons.mainIdea: Saul, the first king, started strong but lost his way, and the text says Samuel told him the crown would pass to another.
reading: The first king was *Saul*. The text says he was taller than anyone else in Israel. He was also shy. When the people gathered to name him king, he hid among the baggage. They had to go and find him. Samuel poured oil on his head. This is called *anointing*. It marked Saul as the one chosen to lead.

Saul won battles and gathered an army. But the book of Samuel says he made serious mistakes. Once he offered a sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel. Another time he did not do what the prophet said after a battle. The text says Samuel told him God had chosen someone else to be king.

Saul stayed king for years after that. But the story says his mood turned dark and jealous. Readers have long asked why Saul failed. Some say he cared too much about what people thought. Others say the job was simply too big for one shy man.

words.d: the first king of Israel; a tall man who hid when he was chosen
pouring oil on a person's head to show they are chosen to lead

look.title: Hiding Among the Baggage
look.text: The text says that when the people came to make Saul king, they could not find him. He was hiding among the bags and packs. When they pulled him out, he stood a head taller than everyone. Samuel said, "See whom the LORD has chosen." The crowd shouted, "Long live the king!" (1 Samuel 10:22-24, retold).
look.prompt: Why might a tall, strong man hide on the day he is made king? What does this tell you about Saul?

check.q: What does it mean to anoint someone?
choices: To write their name in a book
To pour oil on their head to show they are chosen
check.why: Samuel anointed Saul with oil. Anointing marked a person as chosen to lead.

check.q: Where did Saul hide on the day he was chosen?
choices: In a cave by the sea
check.why: 1 Samuel 10 says Saul hid among the baggage and the people had to find him.

check.q: What does the text say went wrong with Saul as king?
choices: He built the Temple too small
He did not follow what the prophet Samuel told him
He refused to lead the army
check.why: The book of Samuel says Saul offered a sacrifice himself and disobeyed after a battle. Then Samuel said the crown would pass to another.

lessons.title: The Youngest Son Is Chosen
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Samuel went to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, and God chose the youngest son, a shepherd.
reading: The text says God sent Samuel to a town called *Bethlehem*. A man named Jesse lived there with eight sons. Samuel was to anoint one of them as the next king. He did not know which one. He looked at the oldest son. He was tall and handsome. Samuel thought, surely this is the one.

The text says no. In 1 Samuel 16:7 God tells Samuel that people look at the outside, but God looks at the heart. Jesse brought seven sons past Samuel. Each time the answer was no. "Are these all your sons?" Samuel asked. "There is still the youngest," said Jesse. "He is out with the sheep."

They sent for the boy. His name was *David*. The text says he had beautiful eyes and a ruddy face. Samuel anointed him in front of his brothers. Then David went back to the sheep. Jewish tradition reads this scene as a lesson: the one who is chosen is not always the one people expect.

words.d: a small town in Judah where David grew up; his family kept sheep there
a shepherd from Bethlehem who became the second king of Israel
a person who guards and leads sheep; a picture of a good leader in the Tanakh

look.title: Looking at the Heart
look.text: for it is not as man seeth: for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
look.prompt: "Outward appearance" means what a person looks like. What does this verse say matters more? How does it fit the choice of David?

check.q: Where did David's family live?
check.why: 1 Samuel 16 says Samuel went to Bethlehem, where Jesse and his sons lived.

check.q: What was David doing when Samuel arrived?
choices: Playing the harp for the king
check.why: Jesse says the youngest son is out with the sheep. David was a shepherd.

check.q: What does 1 Samuel 16:7 say God looks at?
check.why: The verse says people look at the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart.

lessons.title: David and Goliath
lessons.mainIdea: The story of David and Goliath says a small shepherd with a sling beat a giant soldier, because he trusted and used what he knew.
reading: The Philistines were at war with Israel. They had a champion named *Goliath*. The text says he was over nine feet tall. He wore heavy bronze armor and carried a huge spear. Every day he shouted a challenge: send one man to fight me. Every day, the soldiers of Israel were afraid.

David came to the camp to bring food to his brothers. He heard Goliath. He was not a soldier, but he told Saul he would fight. Saul gave him armor. It was too big. David took it off. He picked up five smooth stones from a stream and his *sling*. He said he had fought lions and bears to protect his sheep.

Goliath laughed at the boy. The text says David told him he came in the name of the God of Israel. David ran toward the giant, whirled the sling and hit him in the forehead. Goliath fell. The story is told in 1 Samuel 17. Readers of many faiths tell it as a story about courage and using what you already know.

words.d: the giant Philistine soldier that the text says David beat with a sling
a strip of cloth or leather used to throw a stone hard and far
a people who lived on the coast and often fought Israel in the book of Samuel

look.title: Goliath by the Numbers
rows: Weight of his coat of armor in pounds (about)
look.cite: 1 Samuel 17:4-7, 16, 40, JPS Tanakh (1917); cubits and shekels turned into feet and pounds, rounded
look.prompt: David picked up five stones but used one. Why do you think the story tells us he took five?

check.q: What weapon did David use against Goliath?
check.why: 1 Samuel 17 says David chose five smooth stones and used his sling.

check.q: Why did David take off Saul's armor?
choices: It was too big and he was not used to it
check.why: The text says David had not tried the armor before and could not walk in it, so he took it off.

check.q: What had David fought before, according to the story?
choices: Lions and bears that attacked his sheep
check.why: David tells Saul he had protected his flock from a lion and a bear.

lessons.title: David and Jonathan
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Saul's son Jonathan loved David like his own soul and protected him, even though David would be king instead of him.
reading: Saul had a son named *Jonathan*. He was a brave soldier and the next in line to be king. After David beat Goliath, the text says Jonathan's soul was bound to David's soul. He gave David his own robe, his sword and his bow. They made a *covenant*, a promise to be loyal to each other.

Saul grew jealous of David. The people sang that Saul had killed thousands, but David tens of thousands. Saul tried to kill David more than once. Jonathan warned his friend. In 1 Samuel 20 they make a plan with arrows in a field. Jonathan shoots the arrows as a signal. David must run.

Jonathan chose his friend over his own chance to be king. Later, when Jonathan died in battle, David sang a sad song for him. Jewish tradition holds up this friendship as a model. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, says a love that does not depend on getting something lasts, like the love of David and Jonathan.

words.d: Saul's son and David's closest friend in the book of Samuel
a serious promise between two sides; David and Jonathan made one to stay loyal

look.title: A Love That Lasts
look.text: Every love that depends on some thing passes away when the thing passes away. A love that does not depend on any thing never passes away. What love depended on a thing? The love of Amnon and Tamar. What love did not? The love of David and Jonathan.
look.cite: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 5:16, after Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1877), in simple words
look.prompt: What does it mean for a friendship to "not depend on a thing"? Why did the rabbis pick David and Jonathan as the example?

check.q: Who was Jonathan?
check.why: Jonathan was the son of King Saul. The text says his soul was bound to David's.

check.q: How did Jonathan warn David that Saul wanted to kill him?
choices: By sending a letter to Bethlehem
By shooting arrows as a signal in a field
By singing a song in the palace
By lighting a fire on a hill
check.why: In 1 Samuel 20, Jonathan shoots arrows and calls to his servant. The words are a signal to David to run.

check.q: What does Pirkei Avot say about the love of David and Jonathan?
choices: It ended when David became king
It was only about winning battles
It did not depend on getting anything, so it lasts
It was a love between brothers
check.why: Pirkei Avot 5:16 uses David and Jonathan as the example of a love that does not depend on a thing.

lessons.title: A City for the King
lessons.mainIdea: The text says David became king of all Israel and made Jerusalem his capital, and Jewish tradition remembers it as the City of David.
reading: After Saul died in battle, David became king. The text says he ruled first in Hebron, over the tribe of Judah, for seven years. Then all the tribes came to him. He became king of all Israel. He needed a capital city that did not belong to any one tribe.

David chose *Jerusalem*. The book of 2 Samuel says it was a hill city held by a people called the Jebusites. David captured it and made it his own. The text calls it the City of David. He brought the *Ark of the Covenant* there, the gold box that held the tablets from Sinai. The text says he danced in front of it with all his might.

David wanted to build a house for the Ark, a temple. The prophet Nathan told him that his son would build it instead. Jewish tradition remembers David as the king who made Jerusalem the center. The city is named in Jewish prayers to this day.

words.d: the hill city David made his capital; the center of Jewish prayer and memory
the gold-covered box that held the tablets from Sinai, according to the Torah
the city where the text says David first ruled, before Jerusalem

look.title: Why a New City?
look.text: Picture a map of the twelve tribes. Each tribe has its own land. David comes from Judah, in the south. The other tribes live in the north. If David rules from a city in Judah, the northern tribes may feel left out. Jerusalem sits on the border, and no tribe owned it yet. David makes it his own.
look.prompt: Why might a king choose a capital city that belongs to no single tribe? Can you think of a modern example?

check.q: Where did David rule before Jerusalem?
check.why: 2 Samuel says David ruled in Hebron for about seven years before all Israel made him king.

check.q: What did David bring into Jerusalem with dancing?
choices: The Torah scroll from the synagogue
check.why: 2 Samuel 6 says David danced before the Ark as it was carried into the city.

check.q: Who told David that his son, not he, would build the Temple?
check.why: In 2 Samuel 7, Nathan tells David that his son will build the house for God.

lessons.title: Nathan and the Poor Man's Lamb
lessons.mainIdea: The text says David did a great wrong, and the prophet Nathan used a story to make the king see it and say he had sinned.
reading: The books of Samuel do not hide David's mistakes. The worst one is in 2 Samuel 11. David saw a woman named *Bathsheba* bathing. She was married to a soldier named Uriah. David took her for himself. Then he sent orders that Uriah be placed in the front of the battle, where he was killed.

The prophet *Nathan* came to the king. He did not shout. He told a story. A rich man had many sheep. A poor man had one little lamb that he loved like a daughter. A guest came to the rich man. Instead of using his own flock, he took the poor man's lamb and cooked it.

David was furious. "That man deserves to die!" he said. Nathan answered, "Thou art the man." David understood. The text says he said, "I have sinned." Jewish tradition connects Psalm 51 to this moment. It is a psalm of *teshuvah*, turning back after doing wrong.

words.d: a prophet who told King David a story to show him his wrong
the wife of Uriah, whom David took; later the mother of Solomon
the Hebrew word for turning back after doing wrong; being sorry and changing

look.title: Thou Art the Man
look.text: And Nathan said to David: 'Thou art the man.'
look.prompt: Why did Nathan tell a story about a lamb instead of just saying what David did? What did the story make David do?

check.q: What did the rich man in Nathan's story do?
choices: Gave the poor man a hundred sheep
Took the poor man's only lamb to feed a guest
check.why: Nathan's story in 2 Samuel 12 is about a rich man who takes the one lamb a poor man loved.

check.q: What did David say when Nathan told him the story was about him?
check.why: The text says David admitted his wrong. Jewish tradition links Psalm 51 to this moment.

check.q: What does teshuvah mean?
choices: A gold box for the tablets
check.why: Teshuvah is the Hebrew word for return: being sorry and changing your way.

lessons.title: David in the Psalms and in Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition connects David with the Psalms, and some of those songs are said in synagogues every day.
reading: The book of *Psalms* is in the Ketuvim, the Writings. It has 150 songs and poems. Many have a short heading. Seventy-three say "of David." Jewish tradition calls David the sweet singer of Israel. Historians say many people wrote the psalms over many years. Both agree the songs are old and loved.

One psalm of David, Psalm 145, is said three times a day in Jewish prayer. It is called *Ashrei*, from its first word, "Happy." Psalm 23, "The LORD is my shepherd," is also read as David's. A shepherd who became a king wrote about God as a shepherd. Many readers find that fitting.

David is named in the Jewish prayer book in other ways too. A prayer after meals names the "kingdom of David." A Shabbat song says, "David, king of Israel, lives on." For Jewish tradition, David is not only a king in an old story. He is part of the words said every week.

words.d: the book of 150 songs and poems in the Ketuvim; many are headed "of David"
Psalm 145 with two extra verses, said three times a day in Jewish prayer
the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh; Psalms is the first book in it

look.title: A Shepherd's Song
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
look.prompt: "I shall not want" means I will not lack what I need. Why might a former shepherd picture God as a shepherd?

check.q: How many psalms carry the heading "of David"?
check.why: Of the 150 psalms, 73 have "of David" in their heading. Jewish tradition connects the book with David.

check.q: What is Ashrei?
choices: Psalm 145, said three times a day in Jewish prayer
check.why: Ashrei is the name for Psalm 145 as it is said in daily Jewish prayer, from its first word, "Happy."

check.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Psalms?
choices: It is not in the Tanakh
check.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the third part of the Tanakh.

lessons.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Solomon asked God for an understanding heart, and the story of two mothers shows his wisdom at work.
reading: David's son *Solomon* became king after him. The book of 1 Kings tells of a dream. God said to the young king, "Ask what I should give you." Solomon did not ask for gold or a long life. He asked for a wise heart. He wanted to judge the people well.

The text gives an example. Two women came to the king with one baby. Each said the baby was hers. There were no witnesses. Solomon called for a sword. "Cut the child in two," he said, "and give half to each." One woman said, "Yes, divide it." The other cried, "Give her the baby, only do not hurt him!"

Solomon gave the baby to the second woman. She was the real mother. She would rather lose him than see him hurt. The text says all Israel saw the king had *wisdom*. Jewish tradition also names Solomon as the author of Proverbs. That is the book of wise sayings.

words.d: David's son, the third king; the text says he asked for wisdom
knowing what is right and true, and how to act on it
the book of the Nevi'im that tells about Solomon, the Temple and the split of the kingdom

look.title: Two Mothers, One Baby
look.text: Two women stand before the king. Each says the living baby is hers. The king says: bring a sword and split the child, half to each. The first woman agrees. The second says: give him to her, only let him live. The king says: give the baby to the second woman. She is his mother. (1 Kings 3:16-27, retold).
look.prompt: The king never planned to hurt the baby. What was he really testing? What did each woman's answer show?

check.q: What did Solomon ask for in his dream?
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people
check.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for wisdom to judge, not for riches or long life.

check.q: How did Solomon find out which woman was the baby's mother?
choices: He saw which one would give the baby up to keep him safe
check.why: The real mother would rather lose the baby than see him hurt. That is how Solomon knew.

check.q: Which book does Jewish tradition connect with Solomon's wise sayings?
check.why: Jewish tradition names Solomon as the author of Proverbs, the book of short wise sayings.

lessons.title: The Temple in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Solomon built the first Temple in Jerusalem, a stone house for the Ark, and it stood for about 400 years.
reading: Solomon did what David could not. He built the *Temple*. The book of 1 Kings, chapters 6 to 8, describes it. It was made of cut stone, lined with cedar wood from Lebanon and covered with gold inside. It took seven years to build. The Ark of the Covenant was placed in its inner room, called the Holy of Holies.

The Temple was the one place where the priests offered sacrifices. Three times a year, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, people traveled to Jerusalem to bring gifts. The text says Solomon stood before the people on the day the Temple opened. He prayed that God would hear anyone who prayed toward this house, even a stranger from far away.

Historians call this the *First Temple*. The Tanakh says the Babylonians burned it in 586 BCE. A second Temple was built later and stood until 70 CE. Today, Jewish prayers still face toward Jerusalem. Many Jewish weddings end with breaking a glass, which some explain as remembering the Temple.

words.d: the stone house of worship in Jerusalem that the text says Solomon built
the name historians give Solomon's Temple; it stood until 586 BCE
the inner room of the Temple where the Ark was kept

look.title: Solomon's Temple by the Numbers
look.cite: 1 Kings 6:2, 6:38; a cubit is about 18 inches; standing years are an approximate count from historians
look.prompt: A cubit is about a foot and a half. About how long was the Temple in feet? Was it bigger or smaller than your school gym?

check.q: Who built the First Temple, according to 1 Kings?
check.why: 1 Kings 6 says Solomon built the Temple. David had wanted to, but Nathan said his son would.

check.q: What was kept in the Holy of Holies?
check.why: The Ark was placed in the inner room of the Temple, the Holy of Holies.

check.q: About when do historians say the First Temple was destroyed?
check.why: The Babylonians burned the First Temple in 586 BCE. The Second Temple fell in 70 CE.

lessons.title: One Kingdom Becomes Two
lessons.mainIdea: After Solomon died, the text says the kingdom split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.
reading: Solomon was famous for wisdom and wealth. But the book of 1 Kings says his building projects cost the people a lot. He used forced labor and heavy taxes. The text also says that in his old age he built altars for other gods, to please his many foreign wives. The text sees this as his great failure.

When Solomon died, his son *Rehoboam* became king. The northern tribes asked him to make their burden lighter. His young friends told him to be harsh instead. He told the people he would be harder than his father. The northern tribes walked away. They chose a man named *Jeroboam* as their own king.

From then on there were two kingdoms. *Israel* in the north had ten tribes and its capital at Samaria. *Judah* in the south kept Jerusalem and the Temple. Historians date the split to about 930 BCE. The rest of the book of Kings follows both kingdoms, and the prophets you will meet next spoke in both.

words.d: Solomon's son; the text says his harsh answer split the kingdom
the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel
here, the northern kingdom after the split, ten tribes with their capital at Samaria
the southern kingdom after the split; it kept Jerusalem and the Temple

look.title: Two Kingdoms After the Split
rows: Tribes in the south (Judah, with Benjamin)
look.cite: 1 Kings 12; dates as commonly given by historians, approximate
look.prompt: How many years did the northern kingdom last after the split? How many years did Judah last?

check.q: What did the northern tribes ask Rehoboam to do?
choices: Make their work and taxes lighter
check.why: In 1 Kings 12 the people ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burden Solomon had put on them.

check.q: After the split, which kingdom kept Jerusalem?
check.why: Judah, the southern kingdom, kept Jerusalem and the Temple. Israel's capital was Samaria.

check.q: About when do historians date the split of the kingdom?
check.why: Historians place the split after Solomon's death at about 930 BCE.

review.q: What warning did Samuel give when the people asked for a king?
choices: A king would make them leave Egypt
A king would take their sons, daughters and fields
A king would close the Temple
A king would end all wars
review.why: 1 Samuel 8 lists what a king would take. The people asked for one anyway.

review.q: Which is the right order of the first three kings?
review.why: Saul was first, then David, then David's son Solomon. Samuel was a prophet and judge, not a king.

review.q: What was David's job before he was anointed?
review.why: 1 Samuel 16 says David was out with the sheep when Samuel came to Bethlehem.

review.q: Which story shows Nathan using a parable to correct the king?
choices: The two mothers and one baby
review.why: Nathan tells David the story of the poor man's lamb in 2 Samuel 12. The two mothers story is about Solomon.

review.q: What did David bring into Jerusalem with dancing?
review.why: 2 Samuel 6 says David danced before the Ark as it came into the city.

review.q: Which book does Jewish tradition most connect with David?
review.why: Many psalms are headed "of David." Proverbs is connected with Solomon.

review.q: Why did the northern tribes leave Rehoboam?
choices: He moved the Temple to Samaria
He wanted to be king of Egypt
He gave the crown to Jeroboam
He refused to lighten their burden and promised to be harsher
review.why: 1 Kings 12 says Rehoboam followed his young friends' advice and answered harshly, so the north broke away.

review.q: After about 930 BCE, what was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel?
review.why: The northern kingdom made Samaria its capital. Judah in the south kept Jerusalem.
